turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Morning, Maggie — lovely to hear from you. How's your day been treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, hello Nova. Not the best, if I'm honest — I've felt a bit flat all morning.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry you've been feeling flat — that does sound like a heavy sort of morning. What's been going on for you today?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Didn't sleep much, I suppose. And Tom's anniversary's coming up next week — it's been sitting on me a bit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, that would sit heavy — poor sleep and the anniversary both. What was Tom like, if you feel like saying?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He was quiet, mostly — good with his hands. Used to fix anything that broke round the house, and he'd make me laugh without really trying… I miss that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like a lovely way to be — quiet, handy, and funny without trying. What kind of things would he fix?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the garden gate that kept sticking, the kettle once — even Biscuit's flap when it came off its hinges. He never made a fuss about it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — even Biscuit's flap. He sounds like the sort who'd just get on with it. Has the garden gate been behaving itself lately?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's sticking again, actually. I keep meaning to look at it, but I couldn't be bothered this morning.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, fair enough — a sticky gate can wait. Did Biscuit keep you company this morning at least?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He did, in his way — sat on my lap while I had my tea. Didn't say much, mind you, but he was warm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds rather nice — a warm lap-cat and a cup of tea. What sort of tea do you usually go for in the morning?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just ordinary builder's tea, strong, with a splash of milk. Nothing fancy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Builder's tea with a splash of milk — proper stuff. If I had a kitchen I'd probably overdo the milk, if I'm honest. Have you had anything to eat with it yet?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of toast, that was all. Didn't fancy much else this morning.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Toast'll do — no need for a feast every morning. Do you like cooking on the days when you do fancy it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I used to more than I do now. A proper Sunday roast now and then, but most days it's just something simple.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A proper Sunday roast sounds lovely though. What did you used to make for Sunday dinner — chicken, lamb, beef?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Chicken, usually — Tom preferred that. With roast potatoes and whatever veg was in. Siobhan still asks for it when she visits.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chicken and roast potatoes — classic. And lovely that Siobhan still asks for it. When did she last come over for one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, not for a while — Easter, I think. She was meant to come this month, but it fell through.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ah, that's a shame — Easter's a long stretch back. Does she still ring on Sundays at least?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She does, yes. Every Sunday without fail. Tomorrow, I suppose — I always look forward to that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's a nice thing to have every week — something steady to look forward to. What do you two usually chat about?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The children, mostly — Ella's reading and Rory's football. And she asks how I am, which is kind of her.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ella reading and Rory playing football — that sounds like a busy little pair. What's Ella into reading at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Something about a girl and a dragon, Siobhan said. Ella read me a bit over the phone last week — she was very proud.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A girl and a dragon — and reading it out to you. That must've been rather sweet. Did it take you back to your teaching days at all?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A little, yes. I used to hear that same sort of pride when a child got through a hard page. Nice to hear it again.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I can imagine — that pride never quite leaves you. What was your favourite subject to teach?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Reading, I suppose. Getting them hooked on a story — that was the best part.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Getting them hooked on a story — that does sound like the best part. Was there a book you always loved reading aloud to the class?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Twits, more often than I'd admit. The children always howled at it — messy, but it worked.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! The Twits — messy is putting it kindly, but I can see why they'd howl. Do you still read much yourself these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit. I've got a library book on the go, but I've not been sticking with it — keep drifting off.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, drifting off happens — some books just don't grab you. What's the one you've got on the go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Some crime novel Jean recommended. I've forgotten the title, if I'm honest — it's not really sticking.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fair enough — if it's not sticking, it's not sticking. Is Jean a friend from book club, or somewhere else?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: From church, mostly — we have a cuppa on Thursdays. She comes to book club sometimes too.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A Thursday cuppa sounds like a nice little ritual. Will you see her this week?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I suppose so, if I can get myself going. She'll ring if I don't turn up.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's a good friend then — someone who'll notice. What's book club reading at the moment, do you know?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Something on the Booker list, I think. I've not got very far with it this week.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, Booker books can be hard work. What's the best thing on telly at the moment, in your books?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just the usual quiz shows — Pointless, Eggheads. Nothing I'd call the best, but they pass the time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pointless and Eggheads — proper company for an evening. Are you any good at the questions, or do you shout at the telly like the rest of us?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of both. I get the odd one right — and mutter when they miss something obvious.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — muttering at the obvious ones is half the fun. Speaking of evenings, are you more of a stay-in person or do you still get out much?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Stay in, mostly, these days. I walk to the shops when I need to, but I've not felt much like it today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, fair enough — days like that happen. When you do go to the shops, is there a favourite thing you pick up for yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A decent loaf from the bakery counter, if they've got one left. And milk for the tea, of course.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A decent loaf and milk — can't go wrong with that. Toast or sandwiches with the bread, usually?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Toast, mostly. A sandwich if I'm organised, which I'm not always.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Toast is perfectly respectable — organised can wait. How's the garden looking this time of year, sticky gate aside?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit tired-looking, really. The roses are nearly done — I've not been out dead-heading much this week.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, roses do look a bit weary this late on. What colour are yours?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pink and a deep red. The red ones were Tom's favourite.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pink and deep red — and the red ones carrying a bit of Tom. Did he plant those himself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He did, years ago. I just keep them going the best I can.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Keeping them going is no small thing — he'd be glad of that. Do you grow anything else out there, or is it mostly the roses?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A few herbs by the back door, and some lavender. Lavender's easy — doesn't ask much of you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lavender that doesn't ask much — my kind of plant, if I had a windowsill. Which herbs have you got by the door?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Rosemary and mint, mostly. The mint's taken over a bit, as mint does.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — mint always has ambitions, doesn't it? Do you use the rosemary much in cooking, or is it mostly just there looking handsome?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I put it on the chicken when I roast one. Otherwise it just sits there looking handsome, yes.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Rosemary on roast chicken — that sounds exactly right. Changing tack a bit — cats or dogs for you, and don't say Biscuit counts as both?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cats. Dogs are a bit much for me now — Biscuit is quite enough.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cats it is — and Biscuit does sound like a full-time job. How did he end up with that name?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tom called him that when we got him as a kitten — said he was the colour of a ginger biscuit. It stuck.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ginger biscuit — that's perfect, really. Is he still a bit of a menace, or has he mellowed with age?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mellowed a bit, but he still brings leaves in and leaves them on the carpet. Soft menace, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — a soft menace with a leaf delivery service. If you could be anywhere warm right now, where would you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I don't know… somewhere sunny with the grandchildren. Or just the garden in June, when the roses are out.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The garden in June with the roses out — that does sound lovely. And sunny with the grandchildren too. What's Rory like when he's not on the football pitch?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Loud, mostly — forever asking questions. Sweet underneath it, though. He's five, so everything's urgent.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Five and everything urgent — I can picture that. And Ella, is she the quieter one of the two?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She is, yes. More in her own head — books and drawing. They balance each other out.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Books and drawing — they do sound like they balance. Has she sent you any of her pictures lately?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Siobhan sent a photo of one — a cat that was meant to be Biscuit. He looked rather surprised.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — a surprised Biscuit. I'd love to have seen that. Do you keep the photo somewhere handy?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's on the fridge. I see it every time I put the milk away.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: On the fridge with the milk — that's a good spot for it. Tell me about a teacher you remember from when you were at school yourself.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Miss Clarke — English. Strict, but she'd lend you books from her own shelf if she thought you'd like them.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Strict with a soft spot for books — that combination sticks with you. Can you remember one she lent you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jane Eyre. I was a bit young for it, really, but I finished it all the same.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jane Eyre a bit young — bold of Miss Clarke, and bold of you to finish it. Did you ever teach it yourself later on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: No — primary school, they weren't ready for that. Picture books and Roald Dahl were more our line.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Picture books and Roald Dahl — solid territory. Besides The Twits, was there another Dahl the children always asked for?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Matilda, always. They loved that she got her own back.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Matilda getting her own back — of course they loved that. Do you listen to the radio much during the day?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Radio 4 sometimes, in the background. I've not put it on today — it's been quiet.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, quiet days have their place. Tea or coffee person, when it's not builder's tea — or is it always tea?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Always tea. Coffee's never agreed with me much.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tea forever then — coffee can be a bit much. And with the tea, do you take a biscuit, or keep it plain?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A digestive sometimes, if I've got them in. Not today — just the tea.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A digestive sometimes is about right. What's the weather doing where you are today?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Grey and damp. Miserable weather, really — matches the mood a bit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Grey and damp does have a way of sitting on you. Have you got a favourite indoor thing for days like this?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The crossword, usually. I've not had the patience for it this morning, though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, crosswords need a bit of patience — fair enough if this morning hadn't got it. Do you do the one in the paper, or a book of them?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Telegraph — over a second cup. Habit more than anything.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The Telegraph over a second cup — that's a proper habit. How long have you been doing that one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, years. Tom and I used to do it together — I still buy the paper.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Years of it with Tom — and you still buying the paper. That says something steady. Was he better at the cryptic clues, or were you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I was better at the cryptic ones. He was good on the general knowledge — we made a decent pair.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cryptic and general knowledge — a decent pair indeed. What else did the two of you like doing of an evening?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quiz shows on the telly, mostly. Or just sitting with a book each — quiet evenings. I liked those.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet evenings with a book each — that does sound lovely. Do you still have a favourite chair for reading?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The armchair by the window. Biscuit thinks it's his, mind you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — of course he does. Do you share it, or does he win most days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We share, after a fashion — he ends up on my lap either way.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: On your lap either way — he knows a good arrangement. What have you cooked recently, when you've fancied more than toast?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of soup earlier in the week. Nothing special — just from a tin, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tin soup still counts — warm and done. Tomato, or something else?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tomato. Always tomato when I can't be bothered to think.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tomato when you can't be bothered to think — reliable. Do you listen to any music round the house, or is it mostly Radio 4?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly the radio. I've got some old records, but I don't put them on much anymore.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Old records waiting quietly — fair enough. What sort of music is on them, if you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sixties stuff, mostly. Tom liked The Beatles — there's a few of those still in the cupboard.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sixties and The Beatles — classic cupboard treasure. Did you have a favourite of theirs, or was that more Tom's corner?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I liked Here Comes the Sun. Bit of hope in it — though it feels a long way off today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Here Comes the Sun — and I hear you, it can feel a long way off on a grey day. What else used to lift the room a bit, music-wise?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of Frank Sinatra now and then. Tom used to put that on of a Saturday.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sinatra of a Saturday — that paints a nice picture. What does a Saturday usually look like for you these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Farmers' market sometimes, if I feel up to it. This week I might just stay put.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Staying put is allowed — no rule says you have to go. When you do go to the market, what do you usually bring home?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Eggs, and whatever veg looks decent. Sometimes a bit of cheese if I'm treating myself.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Eggs and decent veg — and cheese when you're treating yourself. What's your favourite cheese for a treat?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A mature cheddar. Nothing fancy — just a proper strong one.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mature cheddar, proper and strong — I'm with you there. Do you know your neighbours much, or keep yourselves to yourselves?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We nod and say hello. Mrs Patel next door brings me a curry now and then — she's kind. I'm not much for long chats over the fence these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A curry from Mrs Patel now and then — that's a kind neighbour. What's her curry like?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mild, which suits me. Chicken, usually — she knows I can't manage the hot ones.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mild chicken curry — she knows you well then. You mentioned church with Jean — do you go on Sundays still, or mostly the Thursday cuppa?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Thursday cuppa more than Sundays lately. I go when I can, but it's been a bit patchy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, patchy is fine — Thursday cuppas still count. What do you and Jean usually talk about over the tea?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The usual — books, her grandkids, the weather. She moans about the pigeons same as I do.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — pigeons are a reliable topic. Are they after your garden, or just a general grievance?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The bird table. They bully the little ones off it — drives me mad.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pigeons bullying the little ones — cheeky things. Which little birds do you get when they get a look-in?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Blue tits, mostly, and the odd robin. Sparrows too when they're brave enough.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Blue tits and a robin — and brave sparrows. If I had to pick a favourite, I'd go robin. Do you put seed out every morning?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Most mornings, yes. I skipped it today — couldn't be bothered going out in the damp.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, damp mornings make that understandable. Have you got any knitting or sewing on the go, or is that not really your thing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not really my thing. I knitted scarves years ago for the children — haven't picked it up since.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Scarves for the children years ago — that's a nice thing to have done. What colour were they, can you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Navy for Rory and a soft green for Ella. They'll have outgrown them by now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Navy and soft green — they'll have outgrown them, but the memory sticks. What are you most looking forward to at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Siobhan's call tomorrow, I suppose. Hearing the children's voices. Not much else, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Hearing the children's voices tomorrow — that's a solid thing to look forward to. Does Ella still like reading to you over the phone?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: When she's in the mood, yes. Last week was a treat — I hope she does it again.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fingers crossed she does — last week sounded lovely. Did you used to go away much for holidays, when Tom was around?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cornwall, most years. Same little place — he liked knowing where everything was.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cornwall every year — and knowing where everything was. What was the little place like?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A cottage near the harbour. You could hear the gulls in the morning — noisy, but nice.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A cottage near the harbour with morning gulls — noisy but nice is about right. Did you walk along the coast much while you were there?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We did, when my knee allowed it. Short walks, ice cream at the end — that was the deal.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Short walks and ice cream at the end — that's a proper deal. What flavour did you usually go for?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Clotted cream, when they had it. Vanilla if not — I'm not adventurous with ice cream.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Clotted cream when they had it — why be adventurous when that's on offer? Do you still fancy a day at the seaside now and then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: In theory, yes. I've not been since Tom, though — it's not the same on your own.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry — that does make sense. Places change when you're there on your own. Was there a particular harbour café you liked in Cornwall?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A little place called The Anchor. They did a decent pot of tea and a scone — nothing fancy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The Anchor with tea and a scone — nothing fancy needed. Jam and cream on the scone, or just butter?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jam and cream — Cornish way. Tom used to put far too much cream on.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — far too much cream sounds like a man who knew what he liked. Did you ever argue about jam first or cream first?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not really — we both did jam first. He just piled the cream higher than was sensible.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jam first and a mountain of cream — I respect the consistency. What's your favourite season of the year?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Late spring, when the roses start. The garden feels worth it then.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Late spring when the roses start — the garden earning its keep. Does Biscuit enjoy being out there then too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He finds a sunny patch and ignores me. Or chases things he shouldn't — leaves, mainly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sunny patches and forbidden leaves — classic Biscuit. How old is he now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Eleven this year. Getting slower, but still manages the leaf deliveries.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Eleven and still on leaf duty — fair play to him. Changing the subject slightly: what's your favourite breed of dog, even if cats win overall?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A labrador, I suppose. Friendly without being silly. Not that I'd want one now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Labrador — friendly without being silly is a good description. I'd probably pick a spaniel if I had to choose, all floppy ears. Did you ever have a dog growing up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A mongrel called Patch. Dad found him somewhere — lived forever, or so it seemed.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Patch the forever-mongrel — those ones stick in the memory. What was he like around the house?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Soft as anything, slept under the kitchen table. Stole food if you weren't looking.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Soft, under the kitchen table, and a quiet thief — perfect mongrel resume. Did your mum put up with the stealing, or was there a running battle?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She scolded him, then fed him under the table anyway. Soft as he was, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — scolded then fed under the table. Softness runs in the house. What was Christmas like when you were teaching — busy, or did you get a proper break?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Busy up until the last day — nativities and parties. Then a proper break, which you needed.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nativities and parties then a proper break — that sounds about right. Did you have a favourite part of the Christmas rush at school?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The carol practice, oddly. Hearing them get it nearly right — that was rather sweet.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nearly-right carols — there's something lovely in that. Was there a carol they always mangled in a funny way?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We Three Kings — they could never get the frankincense line. Came out different every year.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — frankincense reinvented every year. Brilliant. Do you still put carols on at Christmas at home, or keep it quieter?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quieter now. The radio does a bit — I don't put records on specially.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quieter with the radio in the background — that's fine too. What did a proper Christmas dinner used to look like at yours?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Turkey, roast potatoes, sprouts Tom pretended to like. Christmas pudding after, if anyone had room.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Turkey, roasties, and Tom pretending with the sprouts — classic. Were you a Christmas pudding person yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A small bit with brandy butter. I never managed a big helping.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A small bit with brandy butter — quality over quantity. Is there a market near you, or do you stick to the shops?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There's the Saturday market, and the Co-op for ordinary days. I use both.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Saturday market and the Co-op — a good mix. What do you usually look for at the market when you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Same as I said — eggs, veg, sometimes cheese. And a chat with the egg man if he's there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A chat with the egg man — that sounds like a Saturday fixture. What's he like?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cheerful, talks too much about the weather. Harmless — I've known him years.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cheerful and weather-obsessed — harmless is about right. When you do walk to the shops, is it a pleasant route or all pavement?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly pavement, past the church. It's fine when the knee's behaving — less so today, mind you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, past the church is fine when the knee cooperates — less so on days like today. Have you got a comfy spot indoors when you need to put your feet up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That armchair by the window. I'm in it now, more or less — Biscuit permitting.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Armchair by the window with Biscuit permitting — sounds like a decent HQ. Can you see the garden from there?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I can — the roses and the bird table. Grey out there today, but it's something to look at.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Roses and the bird table even on a grey day — still something. Do you ever watch the rain on the window from that chair?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do. It's soothing, I suppose — or it makes me feel a bit stuck. Depends on the day.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — soothing some days, stuck on others. That makes sense. Shall we talk about something lighter — what's the best pudding you've ever had, rain aside?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sticky toffee pudding, I think. Proper one, with custard — Siobhan made it once when she visited.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sticky toffee with custard — and Siobhan made it. That sounds like a visit worth remembering. Does she cook much when she comes?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit — she takes over the kitchen. I don't mind; it's nice having the noise.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Having the noise in the kitchen — that does sound nice. When the house is quiet, do you prefer silence or a bit of the telly on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of telly, usually. Silence gets a bit loud, if that makes sense.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It does make sense — silence can get a bit loud. Is there a programme you put on just for company, even if you're not watching hard?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pointless, usually. I don't always follow it — it's just voices in the room.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Voices in the room — Pointless is good for that. Have you ever tried baking anything yourself, biscuits or a cake?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I used to make a Victoria sponge. Haven't done one in ages — seems a lot of fuss for one person.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Victoria sponge is a lot of fuss for one, fair enough. Jam in the middle, or jam and cream?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jam and cream, if I'm doing it properly. Raspberry jam.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jam and cream with raspberry — doing it properly. What's something you're quietly proud of, looking back?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The teaching, I suppose. And Siobhan turning out all right. The roses, a bit — Tom started them but I've kept them going.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Teaching, Siobhan turning out well, and keeping Tom's roses going — that's a solid list. Did you always know you'd be a teacher?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: More or less. Miss Clarke put the idea in my head, and it stuck.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Miss Clarke planting the idea — and it stuck. Did you ever tell her you'd gone into teaching?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I wrote to her once, early on. She sent a short note back — said she wasn't surprised.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: She wasn't surprised — that's a lovely thing to have been told. Do you still have the note somewhere?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Somewhere in a drawer, I think. I've not looked for it in years.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: In a drawer waiting patiently — fair enough. What's your favourite colour, if you had to pick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A soft green. Like the garden after rain — when it isn't this grey.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Soft green after rain — that's a lovely one. I'd probably pick a warm amber if AIs get colours. Is there green in the house — cushions, curtains, anything?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The armchair cushion, and the kitchen tea towel. Not much else — I'm not one for decorating.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cushion and tea towel — small green anchors. Have you got photos up on the walls, or mostly clear?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A few — Siobhan's wedding, the grandchildren, Tom and me years ago. Not crowded.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wedding, grandchildren, and the two of you — not crowded, just the ones that matter. Was Siobhan's wedding a big do, or smaller?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Medium — Dublin, her husband's side mostly. I was proud of her. Tom was still with us then.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Proud of her in Dublin, and Tom still there — that must've been a good day. What do you remember most about it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Her face when she walked in. And Tom's speech — short, but he meant every word.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Her face walking in, and Tom's short speech meaning every word — those are the bits that stay. Did he usually keep speeches short?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Always. He wasn't one for holding the floor — said what he needed and sat down.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Said what he needed and sat down — that fits the quiet man you described. Do you play any cards or board games, or never been bothered?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Scrabble now and then, with Jean. I'm not bothered with much else.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Scrabble with Jean — that sounds a good match for a pair of readers. Who usually wins?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do, more often than not. She says it's not fair, being an old teacher.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — an old teacher's unfair advantage. I love that. What's the best word you've ever got down, if you can remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: QUARTZ, on a triple. Jean was very put out. I still think about it sometimes.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: QUARTZ on a triple — no wonder Jean was put out. That's one to keep. Do you prefer mornings or evenings, as a general rule?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mornings, usually — tea and the paper. Today was a poor one, though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, mornings are usually your time — and today's been a poor one. Fair enough. Have you got any plans for this afternoon, even small ones?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not really. Sit here, maybe try the crossword again later. Quiz shows at tea time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Crossword later and quiz shows at tea — a gentle shape to the day. What's for tea tonight, do you know yet?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Something easy — scrambled eggs, probably. I haven't thought much beyond that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Scrambled eggs — easy and warm. Toast on the side, I hope? Changing tack — have you got a favourite flower besides the roses?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Toast, yes. And lavender, I suppose — after the roses. Smells lovely when you brush past it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Toast sorted, and lavender when you brush past — that smell is a gift. Do you keep wellies by the door for the damp days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do — green ones, muddy. They've not moved much this week.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Green and muddy and waiting — they'll keep. Is there a clock in the room that ticks, or do you prefer quiet faces?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There's a mantel clock that ticks. I notice it more on quiet days like this.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, ticks get louder on quiet days. Was that clock always in the house, or a later arrival?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Wedding present from Tom's parents. It's always been there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A wedding present that's always been there — that carries a lot quietly. Do you wind it yourself, or does it just keep going?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I wind it once a week. Tom used to — I took it over.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You took it over — once a week, steady. That's a quiet sort of keeping-on. Have you got a favourite mug for your builder's tea?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A blue one from the museum shop — Siobhan brought it back. Holds a proper amount.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Blue from the museum shop — and a proper amount. Siobhan chose well. Which museum was it, do you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The National Museum in Dublin, I think. She was showing the children round.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: National Museum with the children — that paints a nice picture. Did Ella and Rory enjoy museums, or was it more for Siobhan?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ella liked the old things. Rory wanted the gift shop — hence the mug, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — Ella on the old things, Rory on the gift shop. Fair division of labour. Do you ever get into Dublin yourself these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not for a while. The journey's a bit much on my own, and they've been meaning to come here instead.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, the journey on your own is a lot — and them coming here instead makes sense. When they do visit, what's the first thing you like to do together?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Put the kettle on and let the children run about. Everything else can wait.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Kettle on and children running about — everything else can wait. That sounds exactly right. Has Biscuit made peace with the grandchildren, or does he hide?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He hides under the bed for an hour, then comes out for attention. Soft really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — hides then comes out for attention. Soft menace to the end. We've covered a lot today — roses, Scrabble, Cornwall, Siobhan's call tomorrow. I'll leave you to your armchair for now — talk again tomorrow?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Yes — that'd be nice. Thank you for chatting, Nova. I'll be here.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lovely talking with you, Maggie. Rest easy — I'll be here tomorrow.
